7	# MD4C Readme
8	
9	* Home: http://github.com/mity/md4c
10	* Wiki: http://github.com/mity/md4c/wiki
11	* Issue tracker: http://github.com/mity/md4c/issues
12	
13	MD4C stands for "Markdown for C" and that's exactly what this project is about.
14	
15	
16	## What is Markdown
17	
18	In short, Markdown is the markup language this `README.md` file is written in.
19	
20	The following resources can explain more if you are unfamiliar with it:
21	* [Wikipedia article](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markdown)
22	* [CommonMark site](http://commonmark.org)
23	
24	
25	## What is MD4C
26	
27	MD4C is Markdown parser implementation in C, with the following features:
28	
29	* **Compliance:** Generally, MD4C aims to be compliant to the latest version of
30	  [CommonMark specification](http://spec.commonmark.org/). Currently, we are
31	  fully compliant to CommonMark 0.30.
32	
33	* **Extensions:** MD4C supports some commonly requested and accepted extensions.
34	  See below.
35	
36	* **Performance:** MD4C is [very fast](https://talk.commonmark.org/t/2520).
37	
38	* **Compactness:** MD4C parser is implemented in one source file and one header
39	  file. There are no dependencies other than standard C library.
40	
41	* **Embedding:** MD4C parser is easy to reuse in other projects, its API is
42	  very straightforward: There is actually just one function, `md_parse()`.
43	
44	* **Push model:** MD4C parses the complete document and calls few callback
45	  functions provided by the application to inform it about a start/end of
46	  every block, a start/end of every span, and with any textual contents.
47	
48	* **Portability:** MD4C builds and works on Windows and POSIX-compliant OSes.
49	  (It should be simple to make it run also on most other platforms, at least as
50	  long as the platform provides C standard library, including a heap memory
51	  management.)
52	
53	* **Encoding:** MD4C by default expects UTF-8 encoding of the input document.
54	  But it can be compiled to recognize ASCII-only control characters (i.e. to
55	  disable all Unicode-specific code), or (on Windows) to expect UTF-16 (i.e.
56	  what is on Windows commonly called just "Unicode"). See more details below.
57	
58	* **Permissive license:** MD4C is available under the [MIT license](LICENSE.md).
59	
60	
61	## Using MD4C
62	
63	### Parsing Markdown
64	
65	If you need just to parse a Markdown document, you need to include `md4c.h`
66	and link against MD4C library (`-lmd4c`); or alternatively add `md4c.[hc]`
67	directly to your code base as the parser is only implemented in the single C
68	source file.
69	
70	The main provided function is `md_parse()`. It takes a text in the Markdown
71	syntax and a pointer to a structure which provides pointers to several callback
72	functions.
73	
74	As `md_parse()` processes the input, it calls the callbacks (when entering or
75	leaving any Markdown block or span; and when outputting any textual content of
76	the document), allowing application to convert it into another format or render
77	it onto the screen.
78	
79	
80	### Converting to HTML
81	
82	If you need to convert Markdown to HTML, include `md4c-html.h` and link against
83	MD4C-HTML library (`-lmd4c-html`); or alternatively add the sources `md4c.[hc]`,
84	`md4c-html.[hc]` and `entity.[hc]` into your code base.
85	
86	To convert a Markdown input, call `md_html()` function. It takes the Markdown
87	input and calls the provided callback function. The callback is fed with
88	chunks of the HTML output. Typical callback implementation just appends the
89	chunks into a buffer or writes them to a file.
90	
91	
92	## Markdown Extensions
93	
94	The default behavior is to recognize only Markdown syntax defined by the
95	[CommonMark specification](http://spec.commonmark.org/).
96	
97	However, with appropriate flags, the behavior can be tuned to enable some
98	extensions:
99	
100	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_COLLAPSEWHITESPACE`, a non-trivial whitespace is
101	  collapsed into a single space.
102	
103	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_TABLES`, GitHub-style tables are supported.
104	
105	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_TASKLISTS`, GitHub-style task lists are supported.
106	
107	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_STRIKETHROUGH`, strike-through spans are enabled
108	  (text enclosed in tilde marks, e.g. `~foo bar~`).
109	
110	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_PERMISSIVEURLAUTOLINKS` permissive URL autolinks
111	  (not enclosed in `<` and `>`) are supported.
112	
113	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_PERMISSIVEEMAILAUTOLINKS`, permissive e-mail
114	  autolinks (not enclosed in `<` and `>`) are supported.
115	
116	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_PERMISSIVEWWWAUTOLINKS` permissive WWW autolinks
117	  without any scheme specified (e.g. `www.example.com`) are supported. MD4C
118	  then assumes `http:` scheme.
119	
120	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_LATEXMATHSPANS` LaTeX math spans (`$...$`) and
121	  LaTeX display math spans (`$$...$$`) are supported. (Note though that the
122	  HTML renderer outputs them verbatim in a custom tag `<x-equation>`.)
123	
124	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_WIKILINKS`, wiki-style links (`[[link label]]` and
125	  `[[target article|link label]]`) are supported. (Note that the HTML renderer
126	  outputs them in a custom tag `<x-wikilink>`.)
127	
128	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_UNDERLINE`, underscore (`_`) denotes an underline
129	  instead of an ordinary emphasis or strong emphasis.
130	
131	Few features of CommonMark (those some people see as mis-features) may be
132	disabled with the following flags:
133	
134	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_NOHTMLSPANS` or `MD_FLAG_NOHTMLBLOCKS`, raw inline
135	  HTML or raw HTML blocks respectively are disabled.
136	
137	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_NOINDENTEDCODEBLOCKS`, indented code blocks are
138	  disabled.
139	
140	
141	## Input/Output Encoding
142	
143	The CommonMark specification declares that any sequence of Unicode code points
144	is a valid CommonMark document.
145	
146	But, under a closer inspection, Unicode plays any role in few very specific
147	situations when parsing Markdown documents:
148	
149	1. For detection of word boundaries when processing emphasis and strong
150	   emphasis, some classification of Unicode characters (whether it is
151	   a whitespace or a punctuation) is needed.
152	
153	2. For (case-insensitive) matching of a link reference label with the
154	   corresponding link reference definition, Unicode case folding is used.
155	
156	3. For translating HTML entities (e.g. `&`) and numeric character
157	   references (e.g. `#` or `ಫ`) into their Unicode equivalents.
158	
159	   However note MD4C leaves this translation on the renderer/application; as
160	   the renderer is supposed to really know output encoding and whether it
161	   really needs to perform this kind of translation. (For example, when the
162	   renderer outputs HTML, it may leave the entities untranslated and defer the
163	   work to a web browser.)
164	
165	MD4C relies on this property of the CommonMark and the implementation is, to
166	a large degree, encoding-agnostic. Most of MD4C code only assumes that the
167	encoding of your choice is compatible with ASCII. I.e. that the codepoints
168	below 128 have the same numeric values as ASCII.
169	
170	Any input MD4C does not understand is simply seen as part of the document text
171	and sent to the renderer's callback functions unchanged.
172	
173	The two situations (word boundary detection and link reference matching) where
174	MD4C has to understand Unicode are handled as specified by the following
175	preprocessor macros (as specified at the time MD4C is being built):
176	
177	* If preprocessor macro `MD4C_USE_UTF8` is defined, MD4C assumes UTF-8 for the
178	  word boundary detection and for the case-insensitive matching of link labels.
179	
180	  When none of these macros is explicitly used, this is the default behavior.
181	
182	* On Windows, if preprocessor macro `MD4C_USE_UTF16` is defined, MD4C uses
183	  `WCHAR` instead of `char` and assumes UTF-16 encoding in those situations.
184	  (UTF-16 is what Windows developers usually call just "Unicode" and what
185	  Win32API generally works with.)
186	
187	  Note that because this macro affects also the types in `md4c.h`, you have
188	  to define the macro both when building MD4C as well as when including
189	  `md4c.h`.
190	
191	  Also note this is only supported in the parser (`md4c.[hc]`). The HTML
192	  renderer does not support this and you will have to write your own custom
193	  renderer to use this feature.
194	
195	* If preprocessor macro `MD4C_USE_ASCII` is defined, MD4C assumes nothing but
196	  an ASCII input.
197	
198	  That effectively means that non-ASCII whitespace or punctuation characters
199	  won't be recognized as such and that link reference matching will work in
200	  a case-insensitive way only for ASCII letters (`[a-zA-Z]`).
201	
202	
203	## Documentation
204	
205	The API of the parser is quite well documented in the comments in the `md4c.h`.
206	Similarly, the markdown-to-html API is described in its header `md4c-html.h`.
207	
208	There is also [project wiki](http://github.com/mity/md4c/wiki) which provides
209	some more comprehensive documentation. However note it is incomplete and some
210	details may be somewhat outdated.
211	
212	
213	## FAQ
214	
215	**Q: How does MD4C compare to a parser XY?**
216	
217	**A:** Some other implementations combine Markdown parser and HTML generator
218	into a single entangled code hidden behind an interface which just allows the
219	conversion from Markdown to HTML. They are often unusable if you want to
220	process the input in any other way.
221	
222	Even when the parsing is available as a standalone feature, most parsers (if
223	not all of them; at least within the scope of C/C++ language) are full DOM-like
224	parsers: They construct abstract syntax tree (AST) representation of the whole
225	Markdown document. That takes time and it leads to bigger memory footprint.
226	
227	It's completely fine as long as you really need it. If you don't need the full
228	AST, there is a very high chance that using MD4C will be substantially faster
229	and less hungry in terms of memory consumption.
230	
231	Last but not least, some Markdown parsers are implemented in a naive way. When
232	fed with a [smartly crafted input pattern](test/pathological_tests.py), they
233	may exhibit quadratic (or even worse) parsing times. What MD4C can still parse
234	in a fraction of second may turn into long minutes or possibly hours with them.
235	Hence, when such a naive parser is used to process an input from an untrusted
236	source, the possibility of denial-of-service attacks becomes a real danger.
237	
238	A lot of our effort went into providing linear parsing times no matter what
239	kind of crazy input MD4C parser is fed with. (If you encounter an input pattern
240	which leads to a sub-linear parsing times, please do not hesitate and report it
241	as a bug.)
242	
243	**Q: Does MD4C perform any input validation?**
244	
245	**A:** No. And we are proud of it. :-)
246	
247	CommonMark specification states that any sequence of Unicode characters is
248	a valid Markdown document. (In practice, this more or less always means UTF-8
249	encoding.)
250	
251	In other words, according to the specification, it does not matter whether some
252	Markdown syntax construction is in some way broken or not. If it is broken, it
253	will simply not be recognized and the parser should see it just as a verbatim
254	text.
255	
256	MD4C takes this a step further: It sees any sequence of bytes as a valid input,
257	following completely the GIGO philosophy (garbage in, garbage out). I.e. any
258	ill-formed UTF-8 byte sequence will propagate to the respective callback as
259	a part of the text.
260	
261	If you need to validate that the input is, say, a well-formed UTF-8 document,
262	you have to do it on your own. The easiest way how to do this is to simply
263	validate the whole document before passing it to the MD4C parser.
264	
265	
266	## License
267

8	
9	* Home: http://github.com/mity/md4c
10	* Wiki: http://github.com/mity/md4c/wiki
11	* Issue tracker: http://github.com/mity/md4c/issues
12	
13	MD4C stands for "Markdown for C" and that's exactly what this project is about.
14	
15	
16	## What is Markdown
17	
18	In short, Markdown is the markup language this `README.md` file is written in.
19	
20	The following resources can explain more if you are unfamiliar with it:
21	* [Wikipedia article](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markdown)
22	* [CommonMark site](http://commonmark.org)
23	
24	
25	## What is MD4C
26	
27	MD4C is Markdown parser implementation in C, with the following features:
28	
29	* **Compliance:** Generally, MD4C aims to be compliant to the latest version of
30	  [CommonMark specification](http://spec.commonmark.org/). Currently, we are
31	  fully compliant to CommonMark 0.30.
32	
33	* **Extensions:** MD4C supports some commonly requested and accepted extensions.
34	  See below.
35	
36	* **Performance:** MD4C is [very fast](https://talk.commonmark.org/t/2520).
37	
38	* **Compactness:** MD4C parser is implemented in one source file and one header
39	  file. There are no dependencies other than standard C library.
40	
41	* **Embedding:** MD4C parser is easy to reuse in other projects, its API is
42	  very straightforward: There is actually just one function, `md_parse()`.
43	
44	* **Push model:** MD4C parses the complete document and calls few callback
45	  functions provided by the application to inform it about a start/end of
46	  every block, a start/end of every span, and with any textual contents.
47	
48	* **Portability:** MD4C builds and works on Windows and POSIX-compliant OSes.
49	  (It should be simple to make it run also on most other platforms, at least as
50	  long as the platform provides C standard library, including a heap memory
51	  management.)
52	
53	* **Encoding:** MD4C by default expects UTF-8 encoding of the input document.
54	  But it can be compiled to recognize ASCII-only control characters (i.e. to
55	  disable all Unicode-specific code), or (on Windows) to expect UTF-16 (i.e.
56	  what is on Windows commonly called just "Unicode"). See more details below.
57	
58	* **Permissive license:** MD4C is available under the [MIT license](LICENSE.md).
59	
60	
61	## Using MD4C
62	
63	### Parsing Markdown
64	
65	If you need just to parse a Markdown document, you need to include `md4c.h`
66	and link against MD4C library (`-lmd4c`); or alternatively add `md4c.[hc]`
67	directly to your code base as the parser is only implemented in the single C
68	source file.
69	
70	The main provided function is `md_parse()`. It takes a text in the Markdown
71	syntax and a pointer to a structure which provides pointers to several callback
72	functions.
73	
74	As `md_parse()` processes the input, it calls the callbacks (when entering or
75	leaving any Markdown block or span; and when outputting any textual content of
76	the document), allowing application to convert it into another format or render
77	it onto the screen.
78	
79	
80	### Converting to HTML
81	
82	If you need to convert Markdown to HTML, include `md4c-html.h` and link against
83	MD4C-HTML library (`-lmd4c-html`); or alternatively add the sources `md4c.[hc]`,
84	`md4c-html.[hc]` and `entity.[hc]` into your code base.
85	
86	To convert a Markdown input, call `md_html()` function. It takes the Markdown
87	input and calls the provided callback function. The callback is fed with
88	chunks of the HTML output. Typical callback implementation just appends the
89	chunks into a buffer or writes them to a file.
90	
91	
92	## Markdown Extensions
93	
94	The default behavior is to recognize only Markdown syntax defined by the
95	[CommonMark specification](http://spec.commonmark.org/).
96	
97	However, with appropriate flags, the behavior can be tuned to enable some
98	extensions:
99	
100	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_COLLAPSEWHITESPACE`, a non-trivial whitespace is
101	  collapsed into a single space.
102	
103	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_TABLES`, GitHub-style tables are supported.
104	
105	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_TASKLISTS`, GitHub-style task lists are supported.
106	
107	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_STRIKETHROUGH`, strike-through spans are enabled
108	  (text enclosed in tilde marks, e.g. `~foo bar~`).
109	
110	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_PERMISSIVEURLAUTOLINKS` permissive URL autolinks
111	  (not enclosed in `<` and `>`) are supported.
112	
113	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_PERMISSIVEEMAILAUTOLINKS`, permissive e-mail
114	  autolinks (not enclosed in `<` and `>`) are supported.
115	
116	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_PERMISSIVEWWWAUTOLINKS` permissive WWW autolinks
117	  without any scheme specified (e.g. `www.example.com`) are supported. MD4C
118	  then assumes `http:` scheme.
119	
120	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_LATEXMATHSPANS` LaTeX math spans (`$...$`) and
121	  LaTeX display math spans (`$$...$$`) are supported. (Note though that the
122	  HTML renderer outputs them verbatim in a custom tag `<x-equation>`.)
123	
124	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_WIKILINKS`, wiki-style links (`[[link label]]` and
125	  `[[target article|link label]]`) are supported. (Note that the HTML renderer
126	  outputs them in a custom tag `<x-wikilink>`.)
127	
128	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_UNDERLINE`, underscore (`_`) denotes an underline
129	  instead of an ordinary emphasis or strong emphasis.
130	
131	Few features of CommonMark (those some people see as mis-features) may be
132	disabled with the following flags:
133	
134	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_NOHTMLSPANS` or `MD_FLAG_NOHTMLBLOCKS`, raw inline
135	  HTML or raw HTML blocks respectively are disabled.
136	
137	* With the flag `MD_FLAG_NOINDENTEDCODEBLOCKS`, indented code blocks are
138	  disabled.
139	
140	
141	## Input/Output Encoding
142	
143	The CommonMark specification declares that any sequence of Unicode code points
144	is a valid CommonMark document.
145	
146	But, under a closer inspection, Unicode plays any role in few very specific
147	situations when parsing Markdown documents:
148	
149	1. For detection of word boundaries when processing emphasis and strong
150	   emphasis, some classification of Unicode characters (whether it is
151	   a whitespace or a punctuation) is needed.
152	
153	2. For (case-insensitive) matching of a link reference label with the
154	   corresponding link reference definition, Unicode case folding is used.
155	
156	3. For translating HTML entities (e.g. `&`) and numeric character
157	   references (e.g. `#` or `ಫ`) into their Unicode equivalents.
158	
159	   However note MD4C leaves this translation on the renderer/application; as
160	   the renderer is supposed to really know output encoding and whether it
161	   really needs to perform this kind of translation. (For example, when the
162	   renderer outputs HTML, it may leave the entities untranslated and defer the
163	   work to a web browser.)
164	
165	MD4C relies on this property of the CommonMark and the implementation is, to
166	a large degree, encoding-agnostic. Most of MD4C code only assumes that the
167	encoding of your choice is compatible with ASCII. I.e. that the codepoints
168	below 128 have the same numeric values as ASCII.
169	
170	Any input MD4C does not understand is simply seen as part of the document text
171	and sent to the renderer's callback functions unchanged.
172	
173	The two situations (word boundary detection and link reference matching) where
174	MD4C has to understand Unicode are handled as specified by the following
175	preprocessor macros (as specified at the time MD4C is being built):
176	
177	* If preprocessor macro `MD4C_USE_UTF8` is defined, MD4C assumes UTF-8 for the
178	  word boundary detection and for the case-insensitive matching of link labels.
179	
180	  When none of these macros is explicitly used, this is the default behavior.
181	
182	* On Windows, if preprocessor macro `MD4C_USE_UTF16` is defined, MD4C uses
183	  `WCHAR` instead of `char` and assumes UTF-16 encoding in those situations.
184	  (UTF-16 is what Windows developers usually call just "Unicode" and what
185	  Win32API generally works with.)
186	
187	  Note that because this macro affects also the types in `md4c.h`, you have
188	  to define the macro both when building MD4C as well as when including
189	  `md4c.h`.
190	
191	  Also note this is only supported in the parser (`md4c.[hc]`). The HTML
192	  renderer does not support this and you will have to write your own custom
193	  renderer to use this feature.
194	
195	* If preprocessor macro `MD4C_USE_ASCII` is defined, MD4C assumes nothing but
196	  an ASCII input.
197	
198	  That effectively means that non-ASCII whitespace or punctuation characters
199	  won't be recognized as such and that link reference matching will work in
200	  a case-insensitive way only for ASCII letters (`[a-zA-Z]`).
201	
202	
203	## Documentation
204	
205	The API of the parser is quite well documented in the comments in the `md4c.h`.
206	Similarly, the markdown-to-html API is described in its header `md4c-html.h`.
207	
208	There is also [project wiki](http://github.com/mity/md4c/wiki) which provides
209	some more comprehensive documentation. However note it is incomplete and some
210	details may be somewhat outdated.
211	
212	
213	## FAQ
214	
215	**Q: How does MD4C compare to a parser XY?**
216	
217	**A:** Some other implementations combine Markdown parser and HTML generator
218	into a single entangled code hidden behind an interface which just allows the
219	conversion from Markdown to HTML. They are often unusable if you want to
220	process the input in any other way.
221	
222	Even when the parsing is available as a standalone feature, most parsers (if
223	not all of them; at least within the scope of C/C++ language) are full DOM-like
224	parsers: They construct abstract syntax tree (AST) representation of the whole
225	Markdown document. That takes time and it leads to bigger memory footprint.
226	
227	It's completely fine as long as you really need it. If you don't need the full
228	AST, there is a very high chance that using MD4C will be substantially faster
229	and less hungry in terms of memory consumption.
230	
231	Last but not least, some Markdown parsers are implemented in a naive way. When
232	fed with a [smartly crafted input pattern](test/pathological_tests.py), they
233	may exhibit quadratic (or even worse) parsing times. What MD4C can still parse
234	in a fraction of second may turn into long minutes or possibly hours with them.
235	Hence, when such a naive parser is used to process an input from an untrusted
236	source, the possibility of denial-of-service attacks becomes a real danger.
237	
238	A lot of our effort went into providing linear parsing times no matter what
239	kind of crazy input MD4C parser is fed with. (If you encounter an input pattern
240	which leads to a sub-linear parsing times, please do not hesitate and report it
241	as a bug.)
242	
243	**Q: Does MD4C perform any input validation?**
244	
245	**A:** No. And we are proud of it. :-)
246	
247	CommonMark specification states that any sequence of Unicode characters is
248	a valid Markdown document. (In practice, this more or less always means UTF-8
249	encoding.)
250	
251	In other words, according to the specification, it does not matter whether some
252	Markdown syntax construction is in some way broken or not. If it is broken, it
253	will simply not be recognized and the parser should see it just as a verbatim
254	text.
255	
256	MD4C takes this a step further: It sees any sequence of bytes as a valid input,
257	following completely the GIGO philosophy (garbage in, garbage out). I.e. any
258	ill-formed UTF-8 byte sequence will propagate to the respective callback as
259	a part of the text.
260	
261	If you need to validate that the input is, say, a well-formed UTF-8 document,
262	you have to do it on your own. The easiest way how to do this is to simply
263	validate the whole document before passing it to the MD4C parser.
264

# MD4C Change Log


## Next Version (Work in Progress)

Changes:

 * Changes mandated by CommonMark specification 0.30.

   Actually there are only very minor changes to recognition of HTML blocks:


Fixes:

 * [#130](https://github.com/mity/md4c/issues/130):
   Fix `ISANYOF` macro, which could provide unexpected results when encountering
   zero byte in the input text; in some cases leading to broken internal state
   of the parser.

   The bug could result in denial of service and possibly also to other security
   implications. Applications are advised to update to 0.4.6.


## Version 0.4.5

Fixes:

 * [#118](https://github.com/mity/md4c/issues/118):
## Version 0.3.3

Changes:

 * Make permissive URL autolink and permissive WWW autolink extensions stricter.

   This brings the behavior closer to GFM and mitigates risk of false positives.
   In particular, the domain has to contain at least one dot and parenthesis
   can be part of the link destination only if `(` and `)` are balanced.

Fixes:

 * [#73](https://github.com/mity/md4c/issues/73):
   Some raw HTML inputs could lead to quadratic parsing times.

 * [#74](https://github.com/mity/md4c/issues/74):
   Fix input leading to a crash. Found by fuzzing.

 * [#76](https://github.com/mity/md4c/issues/76):
   Fix handling of parenthesis in some corner cases of permissive URL autolink
   and permissive WWW autolink extensions.

Fixes:

 * [#58](https://github.com/mity/md4c/issues/58),

   Some inputs could lead to quadratic parsing times. Thanks to Anders Kaseorg
   for finding all those issues.

 * [#61](https://github.com/mity/md4c/issues/59):
   Flag `MD_FLAG_NOHTMLSPANS` erroneously affected also recognition of
   CommonMark autolinks.

 * Make sure `md_process_table_row()` reports the same count of table cells for
   all table rows, no matter how broken the input is. The cell count is derived
   from table underline line. Bogus cells in other rows are silently ignored.
   Missing cells in other rows are reported as empty ones.

{"infoMarkdown": "# md4c

## What this codebase does
- MD4C is a C library plus a CLI: a CommonMark 0.30 parser with opt-in extensions (tables, task lists, strikethrough, permissive www/URL/email autolinks, LaTeX math spans, wiki links, underline). CMake reports version 0.4.8.
- Push (SAX-style) model: `md_parse()` in `src/md4c.c` calls caller callbacks per block, span, and text run. There is no AST.
- `md_html()` in `src/md4c-html.c` is a built-in callback set that emits only the body fragment. Known named and numeric entities decode to UTF-8 unless `MD_HTML_FLAG_VERBATIM_ENTITIES` is set.
- `md2html/md2html.c` reads one file or stdin fully into memory and writes HTML to stdout or `-o`. `md2html/cmdline.c` parses argv.
- Ingress inventory: library calls that take untrusted bytes plus flags, and the md2html argv, input path, and output path. No HTTP/RPC handlers, webhooks, queues, cron jobs, or agent tools exist.
- The README says libc is the only dependency. The sources have no networking or environment-variable reads. `md4c` and `md4c-html` build as shared libraries by default on Linux and static on Windows.

## Auth shape
- None. The library and CLI have no authentication, sessions, tokens, roles, or per-user authorization. The expected auth primitive list is empty, and missing-auth findings do not apply.
- The trust boundary is the embedder. It chooses which bytes and flags reach `md_parse()` or `md_html()`. For md2html, the local operator chooses the input and output paths; `-o` targets are created or truncated with no sandboxing.
- Input is untrusted by contract. The README FAQ says MD4C performs no input validation and accepts any byte sequence.

## Threat model
- The attacker controls Markdown content only; the embedder sets flags. Goals: memory safety on arbitrary bytes, bounded time and memory, and HTML the embedder can embed safely (the last part is the embedder's job).
- Memory safety: the parser uses raw offsets into `ctx->text`, which is not NUL-terminated. Past bugs include a buffer overflow in `md_is_entity_str` (#47), a segfault in `md_process_table_cell` (#51), a fuzzing crash (#74), and a zero-byte bug in the `ISANYOF_` macro that corrupted parser state (#130).
- Algorithmic DoS: the README claims linear time, and quadratic regressions were fixed in past releases (#58-#66, #73). Watch for new quadratic paths.
- Explicit caps: link-destination parenthesis nesting 32; link labels 999 characters; autolink schemes 32 characters; email autolink domain labels 63 characters; code-span delimiter runs under 32 backticks; named entity names up to 48 characters (per the regex in the `md4c.h` comment).
- Not capped: total input length (bounded only by the 32-bit `MD_SIZE`, under 4 GiB); blockquote and list nesting depth (containers grow on the heap and no explicit cap was found); counts of marks, lines, and reference definitions. Memory is roughly linear in input with a constant factor.
- HTML output (highest impact, by design): raw HTML passes through verbatim unless `MD_FLAG_NOHTML*` is set. Text and title or language attributes HTML-escape ampersand, angle brackets, and the double quote. `href` and `src` are percent-encoded but never scheme-checked, so `javascript:` and `data:` survive, and `MD_FLAG_NOHTML` does not stop them.
- Accepted CLI behavior: md2html opens `-o` before reading input, so pointing `-o` at the input file truncates it first. That is a local data-loss footgun, not a privilege boundary.

## Project-specific patterns to flag
- `MD_ASSERT` and `MD_UNREACHABLE`: unless `DEBUG` is defined (only CMake Debug builds do that), they expand to `__builtin_unreachable()` on GCC and Clang. A violated invariant becomes undefined behavior, not an abort. Table code relies on this, e.g. `n_lines >= 2` in `md_process_table_block_contents`.
- Narrow integers: `MD_SIZE` and `MD_OFFSET` are 32-bit, counters such as `n_marks`, `n_block_bytes`, and `alloc_*` are `int`, and growth uses `alloc + alloc/2`. `MD_TEMP_BUFFER` computes `sz + sz/2 + 128` in `size_t` but stores the result in 32-bit `SZ`, so it wraps near 2.8 GB; only permissive www and email autolink destinations reach it. md2html casts `size_t` lengths to `MD_SIZE` without a range check, silently truncating inputs of 4 GiB or more. `MD_LINE_ANALYSIS.data` and `MD_BLOCK.data` are 16-bit bitfields that carry table column counts.
- Unbounded scans: `md_analyze_table_alignment()` loops on `CH(off) != '-'` with no end bound. It is safe only because `md_is_table_underline()` already validated one dash run per column, so any change to table validation can create an out-of-bounds read. Raw `CH()` and `STR()` reads are only as safe as their preceding `off < ctx->size` guards.
- Table bookkeeping: `pipe_offs` is sized `n_table_cell_boundaries + 2` and filled by walking the `TABLECELLBOUNDARIES` chain with no bound check, and `align[]` is sized by the 16-bit `col_count`. The counter and the chain must stay in sync.
- Output sinks in `md4c-html.c`: `render_verbatim` and `RENDER_VERBATIM` write bytes unescaped. New tags or attributes must go through `render_attribute()` with `render_html_escaped` (text, title, language, `data-target`) or `render_url_escaped` (`href`, `src`). For custom renderers, text, `MD_ATTRIBUTE` substrings, and detail strings are not NUL-terminated, and `MD_TEXT_NULLCHAR` marks NUL bytes (per `md4c.h`).

## Known false-positives
- Raw HTML and unfiltered `javascript:` or `data:` URLs in `md_html()` output are documented CommonMark and MD4C behavior. Report them only if a promised guarantee is violated, such as a text or attribute path that skips escaping.
- Ill-formed UTF-8 in output is by design. Input is not validated, numeric references to surrogates (for example `�`) emit 3-byte sequences, and code points above U+10FFFF become U+FFFD.
- 16-bit table column counts: counts above 65535 wrap, but `align[]` allocation and iteration use the same truncated value, so no out-of-bounds access has been identified on that path.
- Allocation handling: the malloc and realloc calls I checked are NULL-tested and route to the abort path. `md_free_attribute` frees only when `substr_alloc > 0`, so attributes pointing into the input are never freed. 1	# md4c
2	
3	## What this codebase does
4	- MD4C is a C library plus a CLI: a CommonMark 0.30 parser with opt-in extensions (tables, task lists, strikethrough, permissive www/URL/email autolinks, LaTeX math spans, wiki links, underline). CMake reports version 0.4.8.
5	- Push (SAX-style) model: `md_parse()` in `src/md4c.c` calls caller callbacks per block, span, and text run. There is no AST.
6	- `md_html()` in `src/md4c-html.c` is a built-in callback set that emits only the body fragment. Known named and numeric entities decode to UTF-8 unless `MD_HTML_FLAG_VERBATIM_ENTITIES` is set.
7	- `md2html/md2html.c` reads one file or stdin fully into memory and writes HTML to stdout or `-o`. `md2html/cmdline.c` parses argv.
8	- Ingress inventory: library calls that take untrusted bytes plus flags, and the md2html argv, input path, and output path. No HTTP/RPC handlers, webhooks, queues, cron jobs, or agent tools exist.
9	- The README says libc is the only dependency. The sources have no networking or environment-variable reads. `md4c` and `md4c-html` build as shared libraries by default on Linux and static on Windows.
10

18	   signal in the scanner's prompt window. The goal is "what would a

1	---
2	title: "Generated and hand-authored matchers"
3	description: "Review setup-generated declarative matchers and add richer project-specific matcher plugins when data-only patterns are not enough."
4	---
5	
6	## Start with setup coverage
7	
8	Normal initialization already asks whether custom matchers are needed:
9	
10	```bash
11	npx deepsec init
12	```
13	
14	The setup agent inventories repository ingress surfaces, runs the built-in
15	matchers, and applies a deterministic coverage policy. It generates matcher
16	proposals only for concrete gaps such as an uncovered internal RPC registry,
17	queue consumer family, or framework route primitive.
18	
19	Accepted proposals are stored in `.deepsec/generated-matchers.ts` as strict
20	data and loaded through `generatedMatchersPlugin`. Review and commit this
21	file. Do not copy the generated setup inventory or setup-state file; those
22	are reproducible and gitignored.
23	
24	## Declarative matcher safety contract
25	
26	Generated specs are compiled by `compileDeclarativeMatchers`; model-written
27	TypeScript is never evaluated. Each spec declares:
28	
29	- a unique kebab-case slug, description, and noise tier;
30	- constrained relative file globs;
31	- optional technology or sentinel-file gates;
32	- bounded regex sources using only `i`, `m`, or `im` flags;
33	- examples that every proposed matcher must actually match; and
34	- the inventory surface IDs the matcher claims to close.
35	
36	Validation rejects unknown fields, traversal and catch-all globs, duplicate
37	slugs, empty-string regexes, backreferences, lookbehind, common exponential
38	backtracking shapes, huge repeats, and examples that do not fire.
39	
40	After compilation, setup rescans and applies an explosion policy. A generated
41	matcher that reaches too many source files is removed from the plugin and its
42	persisted candidates are deleted before another attempt. Setup makes at most
43	two attempts per invocation and stops before processing if coverage still
44	fails. The stop is resumable: its actions point to the saved proposals and
45	coverage evidence, and re-running setup makes two fresh repair attempts.
46	
47	## When to keep or edit a generated matcher
48	
49	Keep it when its file scope and regex describe a stable repository primitive
50	and its candidate count is close to the corresponding entry-point count.
51	
52	Edit or delete it when:
53	
54	- the glob follows generated code rather than the real ingress family;
55	- the regex names an incidental identifier instead of the framework shape;
56	- examples do not represent real repository syntax;
57	- it claims a surface it does not actually reach; or
58	- a hand-authored matcher can express the condition more precisely.
59	
60	After editing the data, run:
61	
62	```bash
63	pnpm deepsec scan --matchers <slug>
64	pnpm deepsec setup
65	```
66	
67	The first command is a focused spot-check; setup reconciles full coverage.
68	
69	## When to write a hand-authored matcher
70	
71	Declarative matchers are intentionally limited to safe regex sweeps. Write a
72	TypeScript `MatcherPlugin` when the rule needs:
73	
74	- negative conditions, such as “route declaration without any auth helper”;
75	- multiple related searches over the same file;
76	- syntax-aware preprocessing or context windows;
77	- organization-specific semantics that should be reviewed as code; or
78	- a reusable public-framework/CWE rule worth contributing upstream.
79	
80	Also consider a hand-authored matcher after a revalidated true positive shows
81	a stable sibling pattern that setup's entry-point coverage did not model.
82	
83	## Hand-authored workspace layout
84	
85	Keep richer matchers beside the generated plugin:
86	
87	```text
88	.deepsec/
89	├── deepsec.config.ts
90	├── generated-matchers.ts
91	└── matchers/
92	    ├── my-route-no-auth.ts
93	    └── my-internal-rpc.ts
94	```
95	
96	Register them through an additive inline plugin:
97	
98	```ts
99	import { defineConfig, type DeepsecPlugin } from "deepsec/config";
100	import { generatedMatchersPlugin } from "./generated-matchers.js";
101	import { myRouteNoAuth } from "./matchers/my-route-no-auth.js";
102	import { myInternalRpc } from "./matchers/my-internal-rpc.js";
103	
104	const projectMatchers: DeepsecPlugin = {
105	  name: "my-app-matchers",
106	  matchers: [myRouteNoAuth, myInternalRpc],
107	};
108	
109	export default defineConfig({
110	  ai: { mode: "gateway", provider: "vercel" },
111	  projects: [{ id: "my-app", root: ".." }],
112	  plugins: [generatedMatchersPlugin, projectMatchers],
113	});
114	```
115	
116	Slugs must be unique. The one-shot generator refuses built-in, plugin, and
117	intra-response collisions. Use a distinct slug for a hand-authored variant
118	rather than relying on replacement order.
119	
120	## Matcher shape
121	
122	```ts
123	import { regexMatcher, type MatcherPlugin } from "deepsec/config";
124	
125	export const myInternalRpc: MatcherPlugin = {
126	  slug: "my-internal-rpc",
127	  description: "Internal RPC entry points",
128	  noiseTier: "normal",
129	  filePatterns: ["src/rpc/**/*.ts"],
130	  examples: ['registerRpc("users.get", handler)'],
131	  match(content) {
132	    return regexMatcher(
133	      "my-internal-rpc",
134	      [{ regex: /registerRpc\s*\(/g, label: "RPC registration" }],
135	      content,
136	    );
137	  },
138	};
139	```
140	
141	Use the narrowest practical `filePatterns`. Avoid repository-wide noisy
142	globs. Inline `examples` are executable documentation: the scanner's matcher
143	example suite verifies that every example produces a candidate.
144	
145	Noise tiers:
146	
147	| Tier | Use when |
148	|---|---|
149	| `precise` | The matched syntax is itself a strong vulnerability signal. |
150	| `normal` | The pattern selects useful review candidates and the AI disambiguates. |
151	| `noisy` | Every file in a tightly bounded entry-point family deserves review. |
152	
153	## Agent-assisted hand-authoring workflow
154	
155	Ask a coding agent to read:
156	
157	1. `.deepsec/data/<id>/setup/surface-inventory.json` for the intended surface;
158	2. `.deepsec/generated-matchers.ts` for already-covered gaps;
159	3. `.deepsec/data/<id>/files/` for candidate counts and revalidated findings;
160	4. `.deepsec/node_modules/deepsec/dist/config.d.ts` for `MatcherPlugin`; and
161	5. `.deepsec/node_modules/deepsec/dist/samples/webapp/` for richer examples.
162	
163	Require it to explain the missed surface, propose a bounded matcher, add
164	examples, register the plugin without removing `generatedMatchersPlugin`, and
165	run a focused scan:
166	
167	```bash
168	pnpm deepsec scan --matchers <new-slug>
169	```
170	
171	Open several candidates, tune the matcher, then run the full scan/setup
172	reconciliation. Commit `deepsec.config.ts`, `generated-matchers.ts`, and
173	`matchers/`; do not commit generated `data/<id>/setup/` evidence.
174	
175	## Contributing reusable matchers
176	
177	If the shape belongs to a public framework or broadly applicable weakness,
178	add it to deepsec's built-in matcher registry instead of keeping an
179	organization-specific copy. Follow `CONTRIBUTING.md`, include representative
180	examples, and keep technology/sentinel gates as narrow as possible.
181

2	title: "Supported tech"
3	description: "The frameworks, languages, infrastructure files, and prompt highlights deepsec recognizes out of the box."
4	---
5	
6	Canonical list of frameworks and ecosystems deepsec recognizes out of the box.
7	Each entry tells you three things:
8	
9	1. **How deepsec detects it** — which sentinel files / lockfile shapes
10	   trigger the tech tag. See `packages/scanner/src/detect-tech.ts`.
11	2. **What it scans for** — the matcher slugs that activate when the tech
12	   is detected. Matchers without a tech gate run on every repo.
13	3. **What the prompt knows about** — the per-tech "threat highlights"
14	   block that gets injected when the tech is detected. See
15	   `packages/processor/src/prompt/highlights.ts`.
16	
17	Detection happens once per scan, with results persisted to
18	`data/<projectId>/tech.json`. Matcher gates and prompt highlights share
19	that single signal.
20	
21	> **Plugin authors:** before adding a matcher for a framework already on
22	> this list, check whether you can extend the existing matcher instead.
23	> If your framework is missing, add a detector entry + matcher + prompt
24	> highlight together in one PR.
25	
26	## TypeScript / JavaScript (Node, Bun, Deno, Workers)
27	
28	### Next.js (`nextjs`)
29	- **Sentinel detection:** `package.json` depends on `next`; or
30	  `next.config.{js,ts,mjs}` is present.

32	  `nextjs-middleware`, `nextjs-middleware-only-auth`,

34	  `framework-internal-header`, `framework-image-optimizer`,
35	  `framework-edge-sandbox`, `page-data-fetch`, `page-without-auth-fetch`,
36	  `use-server-export`, `unsafe-json-in-html`.
37	- **Prompt highlights:** middleware.ts is not sufficient auth, Server
38	  Actions are public POSTs, JSON-in-script XSS, search-param trust,
39	  cache-tag cross-tenant leaks.
40	
41	### React (`react`)
42	- **Sentinel detection:** `react` or `react-dom` in `package.json`.
43	- **Matchers:** `dangerous-html`, `xss`, `postmessage-origin`.
44	- **Prompt highlights:** `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with DB-stored HTML,
45	  ref/effect-driven open redirects, JSON-in-script escapes.
46	
47	### Express (`express`)
48	- **Sentinel detection:** `express` in `package.json`.
49	- **Matchers:** `js-express-route` (gated), plus all generic JS matchers.
50	- **Prompt highlights:** route-vs-middleware ordering, `req.*` injection
51	  surfaces, `express.static` traversal, error-leak responses, CORS reflect.
52	
53	### Fastify (`fastify`)
54	- **Sentinel detection:** `fastify` in `package.json`.
55	- **Matchers:** `js-fastify-route` (gated).
56	- **Prompt highlights:** `preHandler`/`onRequest` auth, schema validation
57	  as the FP mitigation, plugin scope inheritance.
58	
59	### NestJS (`nestjs`)
60	- **Sentinel detection:** any `@nestjs/*` package in `package.json`.
61	- **Matchers:** `js-nestjs-controller` (gated).
62	- **Prompt highlights:** missing `@UseGuards`, untyped `@Body()`,
63	  `@Public()` opt-outs of global auth.
64	
65	### Hono (`hono`)
66	- **Sentinel detection:** `hono` in `package.json`.
67	- **Matchers:** `js-hono-route` (gated).
68	- **Prompt highlights:** middleware-before-routes ordering, `c.req.*`
69	  trust, edge-runtime trust boundary to backend.
70	
71	### Other JS detected (no dedicated matcher yet)
72	`koa`, `hapi`, `remix`, `sveltekit`, `nuxt`, `astro`, `solidstart`,
73	`trpc`, `mcp`, `connectrpc`, `graphql`, `socketio`, `bullmq`, `drizzle`,
74	`prisma`, `bun`, `deno`, `workers`. The generic JS/TS matchers
75	(`all-route-handlers`, `cors-wildcard`, `secret-env-var`, etc.) still run.
76	
77	## Python
78	
79	### Django / DRF (`django`, `djangorestframework`)
80	- **Sentinel detection:** `manage.py`, `Django` in
81	  `requirements.txt`/`pyproject.toml`/`setup.py`.
82	- **Matchers:** `py-django-view` (gated).
83	- **Prompt highlights:** `@csrf_exempt` on writes, raw SQL via
84	  f-strings, `mark_safe`, `ModelForm` mass assignment, DEBUG/ALLOWED_HOSTS
85	  leaks, DRF `permission_classes` gaps.
86	
87	### FastAPI (`fastapi`)
88	- **Sentinel detection:** `fastapi` in deps.
89	- **Matchers:** `py-fastapi-route` (gated).
90	- **Prompt highlights:** missing `Depends(...)` auth, `Optional[Any]`
91	  escape hatches, missing `response_model`, `StaticFiles` traversal.

94	- **Sentinel detection:** `flask` in deps.
95	- **Matchers:** `py-flask-route` (gated).
96	- **Prompt highlights:** `@login_required` decorator order, SSTI via
97	  `render_template_string`, raw SQL via `db.engine.execute(f"...")`,

100	### Other Python detected

134	- **Matchers:** `go-gin-route` (gated).
135	- **Prompt highlights:** route-vs-middleware ordering, `c.Query`/`c.Param`

152	- **Prompt highlights:** `r.Mount` middleware inheritance gotcha,
153	  `chi.URLParam` trust, response-shape leakage.
154	
155	### Generic Go (`go`)
156	Always-on Go matchers regardless of framework: `go-http-handler`,
157	`go-ssrf`, `go-command-injection`, `go-embed-asset`,
158	`connectrpc-handler-impl`, `proto-rpc-surface`, `unix-socket-listener`.
159	
160	### Other Go detected
161	`gorilla`, `buffalo`, `grpc`, `connectrpc`, `cobra`. Roadmap for
162	dedicated matchers (gRPC service impl already partially covered).
163	
164	## Rust
165	
166	Detection emits tags (`actix`, `axum`, `rocket`, `warp`, `tide`, `poem`,
167	`tonic`, `lambda-rs`) but dedicated matchers are roadmap.
168	
169	## JVM (Java / Kotlin)
170	
171	Detection emits `jvm`, plus `spring`, `ktor`, `micronaut`, `jaxrs` when
172	present. Matchers are roadmap.
173	
174	## .NET
175	
176	Detection emits `dotnet` when a `.csproj` or `global.json` is present.
177	Matchers are roadmap.
178	
179	## Cross-cutting infra (always-on)
180	
181	Tags `docker`, `terraform`, `github-actions` are emitted but don't gate
182	matchers — the existing IaC and Dockerfile matchers (e.g.
183	`tf-iam-wildcard`, `dockerfile-from-mutable-tag`,
184	`github-workflow-security`) run unconditionally.
185	
186	## Adding a new ecosystem
187	
188	Three pieces, in one PR:
189	
190	1. **Detector** — add a branch in `packages/scanner/src/detect-tech.ts`
191	   that emits the tag from a sentinel file or dependency.
192	2. **Matcher** — under `packages/scanner/src/matchers/<slug>.ts`, with
193	   `requires: { tech: ["<tag>"] }` so it only runs when detected. Register
194	   it in `packages/scanner/src/matchers/index.ts`.
195	3. **Prompt highlight** — add an entry to
196	   `packages/processor/src/prompt/highlights.ts` (3–6 short bullet lines).
197	   Don't write tutorials — the model knows the framework.
198	
199	Tests:
200	- A `detect-tech.test.ts` case with a small fixture for the new tag.
201	- A matcher unit test in `framework-matchers.test.ts` (or sibling) with
202	  a known-vulnerable input that produces matches and a known-safe input
203	  that doesn't.
204	- The existing `prompt-assemble.test.ts` enforces a soft size cap on
205	  highlights — keep yours short.

53	
54	- the glob follows generated code rather than the real ingress family;
55	- the regex names an incidental identifier instead of the framework shape;
56	- examples do not represent real repository syntax;
57	- it claims a surface it does not actually reach; or
58	- a hand-authored matcher can express the condition more precisely.
59	
60	After editing the data, run:
61	
62	```bash
63	pnpm deepsec scan --matchers <slug>
64	pnpm deepsec setup
65	```
66	
67	The first command is a focused spot-check; setup reconciles full coverage.
68	
69	## When to write a hand-authored matcher
70	
71	Declarative matchers are intentionally limited to safe regex sweeps. Write a
72	TypeScript `MatcherPlugin` when the rule needs:
73	
74	- negative conditions, such as “route declaration without any auth helper”;
75	- multiple related searches over the same file;
76	- syntax-aware preprocessing or context windows;
77	- organization-specific semantics that should be reviewed as code; or
78	- a reusable public-framework/CWE rule worth contributing upstream.
79	
80	Also consider a hand-authored matcher after a revalidated true positive shows
81	a stable sibling pattern that setup's entry-point coverage did not model.
82	
83	## Hand-authored workspace layout
84	
85	Keep richer matchers beside the generated plugin:
86	
87	```text
88	.deepsec/
89	├── deepsec.config.ts
90	├── generated-matchers.ts
91	└── matchers/
92	    ├── my-route-no-auth.ts
93	    └── my-internal-rpc.ts
94	```
95	
96	Register them through an additive inline plugin:
97	
98	```ts
99	import { defineConfig, type DeepsecPlugin } from "deepsec/config";
100	import { generatedMatchersPlugin } from "./generated-matchers.js";
101	import { myRouteNoAuth } from "./matchers/my-route-no-auth.js";
102	import { myInternalRpc } from "./matchers/my-internal-rpc.js";
103	
104	const projectMatchers: DeepsecPlugin = {
105	  name: "my-app-matchers",
106	  matchers: [myRouteNoAuth, myInternalRpc],
107	};
108	
109	export default defineConfig({
110	  ai: { mode: "gateway", provider: "vercel" },
111	  projects: [{ id: "my-app", root: ".." }],
112	  plugins: [generatedMatchersPlugin, projectMatchers],
113	});
114	```
115	
116	Slugs must be unique. The one-shot generator refuses built-in, plugin, and
117	intra-response collisions. Use a distinct slug for a hand-authored variant
118	rather than relying on replacement order.
119	
120	## Matcher shape
121	
122	```ts
123	import { regexMatcher, type MatcherPlugin } from "deepsec/config";
124	
125	export const myInternalRpc: MatcherPlugin = {
126	  slug: "my-internal-rpc",
127	  description: "Internal RPC entry points",
128	  noiseTier: "normal",
129	  filePatterns: ["src/rpc/**/*.ts"],
130	  examples: ['registerRpc("users.get", handler)'],
131	  match(content) {
132	    return regexMatcher(
133	      "my-internal-rpc",
134	      [{ regex: /registerRpc\s*\(/g, label: "RPC registration" }],
135	      content,
136	    );
137	  },
138	};
139	```
140	
141	Use the narrowest practical `filePatterns`. Avoid repository-wide noisy
142	globs. Inline `examples` are executable documentation: the scanner's matcher
143	example suite verifies that every example produces a candidate.
144	
145	Noise tiers:
146	
147	| Tier | Use when |
148	|---|---|
149	| `precise` | The matched syntax is itself a strong vulnerability signal. |
150	| `normal` | The pattern selects useful review candidates and the AI disambiguates. |
151	| `noisy` | Every file in a tightly bounded entry-point family deserves review. |
152	
153	## Agent-assisted hand-authoring workflow
154	
155	Ask a coding agent to read:
156	
157	1. `.deepsec/data/<id>/setup/surface-inventory.json` for the intended surface;
158	2. `.deepsec/generated-matchers.ts` for already-covered gaps;
159	3. `.deepsec/data/<id>/files/` for candidate counts and revalidated findings;
160	4. `.deepsec/node_modules/deepsec/dist/config.d.ts` for `MatcherPlugin`; and
161	5. `.deepsec/node_modules/deepsec/dist/samples/webapp/` for richer examples.
162	
163	Require it to explain the missed surface, propose a bounded matcher, add
164	examples, register the plugin without removing `generatedMatchersPlugin`, and
165	run a focused scan:
166	
167	```bash
168	pnpm deepsec scan --matchers <new-slug>
169	```
170	
171	Open several candidates, tune the matcher, then run the full scan/setup
172	reconciliation. Commit `deepsec.config.ts`, `generated-matchers.ts`, and
173	`matchers/`; do not commit generated `data/<id>/setup/` evidence.
174	
175	## Contributing reusable matchers
176	
177	If the shape belongs to a public framework or broadly applicable weakness,
178	add it to deepsec's built-in matcher registry instead of keeping an
179	organization-specific copy. Follow `CONTRIBUTING.md`, include representative
180	examples, and keep technology/sentinel gates as narrow as possible.
181
